newsitem.title: LEBANON: Beirut bans over 150 TV and radio stations.
newsitem.headline: Beirut bans over 150 TV and radio stations.

text.p: The Lebanese government licensed on Tuesday a handful of private television and radio stations out of a mass of media outlets dominating air waves since the 1975-90 civil war.

The cabinet of Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri approved applications of four major private television stations and 12 radio stations, owned by political leaders or businessmen. The cabinet ordered all other stations to close by end of November.

The government did not licence a television and a radio station run by the pro-Iranian Hizbollah group but granted them a special permission to continue operating and broadcast news on a guerrilla campaign to oust Israeli troops from south Lebanon.
However, they were ordered to refrain from broadcasting political programmes or news.
Hizbollah's al-Manar Television and al-Nour radio stations would continue to operate "as long as Israel occupied Lebanese land", the government said.
Hizbollah's military wing, the Islamic Resistance, is fighting to oust Israeli troops from a 15-km (nine miles)-wide south Lebanon occupation zone.

Information Minister Farid Makari said after a three-hour cabinet session that "the cabinet also ordered all private stations that have not been licensed to stop broadcasting news and political programmes as of Wednesday. They are all given until end of November to liquidate their premises".

It licensed the following television stations: Future Television of Hariri, NBN, a station which Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri is reported to be setting up, MTV of the brother of Deputy Prime Minister Michel al-Murr and Lebanon's top private station LBCI.

It also licensed the following three radio stations allowing them to broadcast political programs and news: Hariri's Radio Orient, National Broadcasting Network which Berri is setting up and Voice of Free Lebanon, previously owned by the Lebanese Forces, the main Christian war militia, before it was outlawed. Now it is owned by a group of Lebanese investors.
Estimates of the present number of television stations range between 38 and 57, plus 150 radio stations. Some were militia mouthpieces during the war but have turned commercial since.
Some 63 television and radio stations had lodged applications.
State-run Tele Liban and Lebanon Radio are already licensed.
